author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell's guest broke down a joint agreement between the British government and Moderna, tied to a large investment in a new manufacturing plant near Oxford designed to produce 250 million mRNA vaccine doses a year, covering everything from Covid to flu to RSV. He pointed out the unsettling part, the government reportedly committed to purchasing these products for the next ten years despite limited data on long term efficacy or adverse reactions. Russell noted the strange logic of locking in a decade of guaranteed doses for technology that's still relatively untested, regardless of how it actually performs. Sometimes the commitment gets made long before the results ever do.

author: Russell Brand
description:
An interviewer pushed Elon Musk on why people loathe him, pointing to his wealth and influence over politics as the reason. Musk pushed back, admitting some people probably do hate him but arguing that a quarter billion people follow him, which he took as proof that far more people actually like him than dislike him. He then flipped the question entirely, telling her directly that a lot more people hate her and the media than she probably realizes. Sometimes the sharpest comeback is just turning the question back around.

title: Does anyone actually trust the media anymore?

author: Russell Brand
description:
Jordan Peterson argued that a lot of what passes for morality is really just convention and cowardice, pointing to the public pile-on around a famous golfer's affair as an example. He challenged the men eager to condemn him, suggesting most would behave exactly the same way if given the same opportunity and power, and that claiming celibate virtue simply because no temptation ever arrived isn't morality, it's uselessness dressed up as principle. He went further, arguing you can't really know your own capacity for good or evil until you've been in a position where your instincts had genuine free reign, because until then your character has never actually been tested. Russell listened as he connected it to a wider culture that keeps people passive, atomized, and safely untested by design.
